09-148.r: Microfinance → basic financial services for poor and low-income households: credit, savings, insurance, fund (cash) transfers, leasing (all four given).

09-149.r: RBI sub-committee on microfinance → Y.H. Malegam (formed October 15, 2010); recommended a separate NBFC-MFI category.

09-150.r: Malegam Committee recommendation → new NBFC category: NBFC-Microfinance Institution (NBFC-MFI), 2011.

09-151.r: 'Gullak Bachcha Bank' → run by children at Bal Bhavan-Kilkari, Patna; opened November 14, 2009 by Nitish Kumar for thrift education.

09-152.r: Bank assets → cash, money at call, investments, loans and advances (e.g. credit to farmers); deposits and RBI borrowings are liabilities.
09-152.h: Bank owes deposits (liability); bank is owed loans (asset).
09-152.t: Deposits are a bank's liabilities; loans are its assets.

09-153.r: Deposits are a liability (must be repaid), not an asset; bank assets → cash and RBI balances, money at call and short notice, investments, advances.

09-154.r: Most important liability of commercial banks → time deposits; then savings and demand deposits.

09-155.r: Non-performing asset (NPA) → loan whose interest or principal is overdue for more than 90 days.

09-156.r: Priority sector lending (at least 40% of bank credit) → agriculture, MSMEs, weaker sections, education, housing, export credit, renewable energy.

09-157.r: Loan terms → short-term up to 1 year (or 15 months); medium-term up to 3 (or 5) years; long-term beyond that.

09-158.r: Teaser loans → housing loans with ultra-low initial fixed rate, then market rates; seen as subprime lending with future default risk; not for new entrepreneurs.

09-160.r: Non-financial debt → credit instruments of governments, households, businesses outside financial sector: housing loans, credit card dues, treasury bills (all three).

09-161.r: Core Banking Solutions → networked branches let customers operate accounts from any branch; not RBI control or takeover of NPA-laden banks.

09-162.r: June 2007 → Government of India acquired RBI's 59.7% stake in State Bank of India.

09-163.r: NABARD was under RBI control at question time; RBI divested NABARD (2010, 2019) and NHB (2019) stakes; Government now holds 100% of both.
09-163.c: Answer not printed; explanation points to NABARD (option c).

09-164.r: National Housing Bank (July 9, 1988, NHB Act 1987) → apex housing finance body, wholly owned by RBI till March 19, 2019; now 100% Government.

09-165.r: Basel III → Basel Committee measures after 2007-09 crisis to strengthen bank regulation, supervision, risk management and ability to handle stress.
09-165.h: Basel I 1988, Basel II 2004, then Basel III after the crisis.

09-166.r: Basel II (June 2004) → international bank capital adequacy standards; three pillars: minimum capital, supervisory review, market discipline (disclosure).

09-167.r: CAR (CRAR) → bank capital vs risk-weighted assets, to absorb losses; fixed by central banks/regulators, not each bank; Basel III 8%; RBI 9% (11.5% with buffer).

09-168.r: DICGC → wholly owned RBI subsidiary (Act of 1961); insures each depositor up to Rs. 5 lakh per bank (from 4 February 2020; earlier Rs. 1 lakh).
09-168.h: Deposit cover went from Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 5 lakh in 2020.

09-169.r: Savings account interest rates → deregulated by RBI in October 2011; now fixed by banks themselves, not Finance Ministry or IBA.

09-170.r: MCLR (from April 1, 2016) → internal minimum lending rate; brings transparency in loan pricing and fair rates for borrowers and banks.

09-171.r: RBI → apex bank, regulates money supply, monitors NABARD; does not lend to business families.

09-172.r: RBI (April 1, 1935) → banker to Government, frames monetary policy, Government's agent for IMF membership, manages Government borrowing.

09-173.r: Fiscal agent and adviser to Government on monetary and financial matters → RBI (RBI Act, 1934).

09-174.r: RBI manages both Central securities and State Development Loans (by agreement with States); only Centre issues T-bills, States issue only bonds; T-bills issued at discount, redeemed at face value.
09-174.h: T-bill: bought at a discount, paid back at full face value.

09-175.r: Treasury bills → short-term Government of India debt sold by RBI through auction; first issued 1917; tenors 91, 182, 364 days.
09-175.h: T-bill tenors are about three, six and twelve months.

09-176.r: Retail investors can buy T-bills and G-Secs in primary market (RBI Retail Direct, November 12, 2021); NDS-OM is RBI's G-Sec trading platform; CDSL promoted by BSE, not RBI.

09-177.r: RBI is banker to all State Governments (and UTs Puducherry, Jammu & Kashmir) under Section 21A, RBI Act 1934, except Sikkim (limited debt agreement).
09-177.c: Answer not printed; Sikkim is the only exception and is not among the options.

09-178.r: RBI regulates banks' liquidity of assets (Repo, SLR, CRR), branch expansion (rural-urban ratio), bank mergers (with Competition Commission) and winding-up (all four).

09-179.r: RBI → established April 1, 1935 (RBI Act 1934), not 1949; nationalised 1949; HQ Kolkata, moved to Mumbai 1937; Governments' banker, forex custodian.

09-186.r: Lender of last resort → RBI gives emergency liquidity to solvent banks in temporary crisis; not lending to industry or financing budget deficits.

09-187.r: RBI does not issue all notes: one rupee note issued by Government of India, signed by Finance Secretary; other notes signed by RBI Governor.

09-189.r: Credit creation → function of commercial banks, not RBI; RBI controls credit, frames monetary policy, is apex of scheduled banks.

09-190.r: Foreign trade regulated by Ministry of Commerce and Industry, not RBI; RBI issues currency, banks for banks and government, controls credit, manages forex.

09-191.r: RBI as bankers' bank → banks keep deposits with RBI; RBI lends to them in need and advises on monetary matters. RBI is India's central bank (1935).

09-193.r: Monetary policy complements fiscal policy; it acts indirectly through credit and money supply, fiscal policy acts directly on demand.

09-194.r: Monetary policy objectives → price stability, economic stability, exchange rate stability; equitable distribution of income and assets is not one.

09-195.r: Monetary policy → formulated by RBI till 2016; now Monetary Policy Committee sets policy rate, aided by RBI's Monetary Policy Department; RBI keeps price stability.
09-195.c: Answer not printed; explanation supports RBI (option b), with MPC now setting the rate.

09-197.r: Monetary Policy Committee → decides RBI benchmark rates; six members (three RBI incl. Governor, three Government nominees for four years); RBI Governor chairs.
09-197.h: MPC = three RBI + three Government = six; RBI Governor holds the chair.
09-197.t: MPC has six members, not 12; chaired by RBI Governor, not Finance Minister.

09-198.r: 'Money and Credit' in India controlled by RBI, using quantitative and qualitative measures.

09-199.r: Selective (qualitative) control → margin requirements, consumer credit regulation, credit rationing, moral suasion; quantitative → Bank Rate, OMO (securities sale), Repo, variable CRR/SLR.
09-199.h: Quantitative = how much credit (rates, ratios, OMO); qualitative = where credit goes (margins, rationing).

09-203.r: Monetary policy tools → Bank Rate, open market operations; public debt and public revenue belong to fiscal policy.

09-204.r: Open market operations → RBI buys government securities and T-bills to raise money supply, sells them to cut it.
09-204.h: OMO: Buy = boost money supply; Sell = squeeze it.
hi: Open market operations (खुले बाजार की क्रियाएँ)

09-206.r: Variable reserve ratios and open market operations → tools of RBI's monetary policy to regulate credit and money supply.

09-207.r: Sterilisation → RBI absorbs fresh money (e.g. capital inflows) to curb inflation or currency appreciation, mainly via open market operations (selling T-bills).

09-208.r: Operation Twist → RBI buys long-term and sells short-term securities together to lower long-term rates and promote long-term investment (US Fed first, 1961).
09-208.h: Twist: buy long, sell short at the same time.

09-209.r: Money supply rises when Central Bank buys government securities from public or Government borrows from it; deposits in banks and securities sales reduce it.

09-210.r: RBI fights inflation by raising Bank Rate, Repo, CRR and SLR and selling government securities; buying securities would add money.

09-211.r: High inflation → RBI sells (not buys) government securities; rupee falling fast → RBI sells dollars; lower US/EU rates bring inflows → RBI buys dollars.

09-212.r: Statutory Reserve Requirement → minimum share of deposits kept as cash, gold or securities; lets Central Bank control advances (credit growth) banks create.

09-213.r: SLR → way commercial banks provide credit to Government: banks hold reserves mostly in government securities (Section 24 (2A), Banking Regulation Act 1949).
09-213.t: CRR is cash kept with RBI (no interest); SLR is liquid assets kept by banks themselves.

09-214.r: SLR cut by 50 basis points → banks get more lendable funds and may cut lending rates; SLR = share of deposits kept as cash, gold, securities.

09-216.r: Prime Lending Rate (PLR) → set by commercial banks for best corporate borrowers, not by RBI; RBI fixes Bank Rate, CRR, SLR.

09-217.r: MSF → banks borrow overnight from RBI by dipping into SLR at penal rate; Bank Rate aligned with MSF rate. NDTL → banks' net demand and time liabilities.

09-218.r: Expansionary monetary policy → cut SLR, Bank Rate and Repo Rate; RBI would not raise Marginal Standing Facility rate (makes borrowing costlier).

09-219.r: Lower interest rate → borrowing easier, so investment (and consumption) expenditure rises.

09-220.r: Financial sector reforms → lower CRR and SLR, deregulated interest rates, private entry into banking and insurance, NPA reforms (all options).

09-221.r: After reforms (Narsimham Committee) → SLR cut from 38.5% (1991) to 25% (1997); CRR from 13% (1996) to 9% (1999); now CRR 4.50%, SLR 18%.

09-222.r: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) → mandatory share of banks' deposits kept as cash with RBI.

09-223.r: Higher CRR → fewer loanable funds → less liquidity (money supply) in the economy.

09-224.r: Lower CRR → more bank liquidity, more investment, wider money supply, more credit creation (I, II, III true); real investment rate does not decline (IV false).

09-226.r: Higher CRR → banks deposit more with RBI and have less money to lend; credit creation and money supply fall, curbing inflation.

09-229.r: Repo Rate → key monetary policy rate at which RBI lends short-term money to banks; a monetary (not fiscal) policy tool.

09-230.r: Repo (Repurchase Option) → used by RBI to regulate money supply and inflation, not to handle rupee sell-off in exchange market.

09-232.r: Repo Rate → rate at which RBI lends short-term (overnight) funds to commercial banks against government securities under LAF.
09-232.h: Repo: RBI gives money; Reverse Repo: RBI takes money.

09-234.r: Reverse Repo Rate → rate at which banks lend to RBI (RBI borrows), absorbing surplus money overnight against government securities.
09-234.h: Repo: RBI gives money; Reverse Repo: RBI takes money.

09-237.r: CPI inflation rises when Bank Rate or Reverse Repo Rate is cut; raising Repo Rate or SLR reduces inflation.
09-237.c: Answer not printed; book says (a) and (b) both correct and RPSC's key (d) is wrong.

09-238.r: Higher Bank Rate → costlier borrowing for banks, less money supply; signals tight (contractionary) money policy.
09-238.h: Bank Rate up = tight (dear) money; down = easy (cheap) money.

09-239.r: Lower Bank Rate → banks borrow and lend more → more liquidity in the market.

09-240.r: Bank Rate → rate at which RBI rediscounts bills of exchange, i.e. lends to commercial banks; a monetary policy tool.

09-243.r: June 2010 to June 2011 → Repo minus Reverse Repo = 1.00 percent; from 2011-12 Reverse Repo was set 1% below Repo (no longer so).

09-244.r: RBI policy, December 5, 2019 → Repo Rate 5.15%, Reverse Repo 4.90%; on 7 June 2024: Repo 6.50%, Bank Rate and MSF 6.75%.

09-245.r: Repo Rate on September 30, 2014 → 8.00%; on 7 June 2024 → 6.50% (SDF 6.25%, MSF and Bank Rate 6.75%, CRR 4.50%, SLR 18.00%).

09-246.r: October 2001 → RBI cut Bank Rate by 0.5 percent, from 7% to 6.5%; MSF aligned with Bank Rate from February 2012.

09-247.r: Bank Rate per RBI review of 29 September 2015 → 7.75%; 6.75% as on 7 June 2024.

09-248.r: RBI Governors in order → I.G. Patel → Manmohan Singh → C. Rangarajan → D. Subbarao.

09-249.r: RBI Governor (and up to 4 Deputy Governors) appointed by Central Government; Governor's powers from RBI Act; Centre's power to direct RBI is in RBI Act Section 7, not Constitution.

09-250.r: Raja J. Chelliah was never RBI Governor; Governors: Manmohan Singh (1982 to 1985), C. Rangarajan (1992 to 1997), Bimal Jalan (1997 to 2003).

09-251.r: RBI Governors → Raghuram Rajan (2013–2016), Urjit Patel (2016–2018), Shaktikanta Das (25th Governor, from 12 December 2018).

09-252.r: Committee on Financial Sector Assessment (2006) → chaired by RBI Deputy Governor Rakesh Mohan, co-chaired by Finance Secretary; report March 2009.

09-253.r: RBI accounting year → January–December, then July–June (from 1940), now April–March (from 2020-21, a nine-month transition year).

09-255.r: Negotiable Instruments Act → passed December 1881, in force 1 March 1882; 2018 amendment added sections 143A, 148 to protect payees of dishonoured cheques.

09-256.r: UTI → mutual fund; Canbank Financial Services → Canara Bank subsidiary; SBI → commercial bank; U.P. State Financial Corporation → State Government enterprise.
09-256.c: Answer not printed; book says each option differs from the rest on some basis, so no single answer.

09-257.r: Company limited by shares → members' liability limited to the unpaid amount on their shares (Companies Act 2013).

09-258.r: LLP → limited liability with partnership flexibility; minimum two partners, no maximum; perpetual succession; partners may manage and set governance by agreement.
09-258.t: 'Partners should be less than 20' is wrong: LLP has no upper limit.

09-259.r: International Financial Services Centre → GIFT City, Gandhinagar (Gujarat); IFSCA set up April 27, 2020 under IFSCA Act, 2019.

09-260.r: IFCI (1 July 1948, statutory corporation) → India's first development financial institution, giving medium and long-term finance to industry.

09-261.r: Apex institution for industrial finance → IDBI (July 1964), serving medium and large industries.

09-264.r: Founding years → IFCI 1948; ICICI 1955; IDBI 1964; SIDBI 1990.

09-265.r: Founding years → ICICI 1955; IDBI 1964; Exim Bank 1982 (Act of 1981); BIFR 1987.

09-266.r: Founding years → Allahabad Bank 1865; Alliance Bank of Shimla 1874; Awadh (Oudh) Commercial Bank 1881; Punjab National Bank 1894.
09-266.h: Allahabad Bank is the oldest (1865); PNB the youngest (1894).

09-267.r: SAIL → marketing institution; SEBI (capital market), SIDBI and NABARD (agricultural credit) → apex institutions in their fields.

09-268.r: SBI is a commercial bank, not an apex institution; NABARD, SIDBI and State Cooperative Bank are apex institutions.

09-269.c: Answer not printed; true order 1, 4, 2, 3 matches no option.

09-271.r: IRDAI → from Malhotra Committee; autonomous body 1999; statutory body from April 2000; regulates insurance companies.

09-274.r: IRDAI panel on standard cyber liability insurance product (October 2020) → chaired by P. Umesh.

09-275.r: Actuary → insurance professional who assesses risk and estimates premiums.

09-276.r: Principle of Indemnity (restore insured to pre-loss position) applies to fire and marine insurance, not life insurance.
09-276.h: No indemnity in life insurance: the loss from a death cannot be valued.

09-277.r: Provident Fund → contractual savings: mandatory, government-managed retirement savings from employee and employer contributions.

09-278.r: State Provident Fund receipts → credited to Public Account, not Consolidated or Contingency Fund.

09-279.r: Among private banks, development banks, Exim Bank and pension funds → pension funds' importance has fallen most.

09-280.r: Forward Markets Commission (1953) → regulated commodity futures; merged with SEBI on 28 September 2015.

09-281.r: SEBI → regulates mutual funds and stock markets; non-statutory 1988, statutory April 12, 1992 (SEBI Act 1992); HQ Mumbai.
09-281.h: SEBI: born 1988, made statutory (given teeth) in 1992.
hi: Securities and Exchange Board of India (भारतीय प्रतिभूति और विनिमय बोर्ड)

09-287.r: Private sector mutual funds allowed in 1993 (first: Kothari Pioneer); UTI began the industry in 1964; SBI Mutual Fund first non-UTI fund (1987).

09-288.r: UTI's Unit Scheme 1964 (US-64) in news (1998) → net worth fell sharply; redemptions exceeded sales amid long stock market slump.

09-289.r: UTI (February 1, 1964) → mobilise small savings, share earnings with small investors, invest to promote industrial development; split in two on 1 February 2003.

09-290.r: Largest mutual fund → UTI at question time; now SBI Mutual Fund (by assets under management).

09-291.r: National Stock Exchange → set up November 1992 on Manohar J. Pherwani Committee's advice; head office Mumbai.

09-292.r: NSE promoters → IDBI, SBI, IFCI, LIC, GIC, IDFC; now (31.03.2024) promoter holding is zero.

09-293.r: Sensex → 30 stocks (not 50), market-cap weighted with proportional weightage; oldest stock exchange is Amsterdam, not New York (1792).

09-294.r: Rise in SENSEX → overall rise in share prices of its group of 30 companies on Bombay Stock Exchange (free-float market-weighted).

09-297.r: BSE Greenex → 25 top 'green' companies by greenhouse gas emissions, market cap and liquidity.

09-299.r: Highest turnover in 2000-01 → National Stock Exchange (8.39 lakh crore); NSE still has the highest turnover.

09-300.r: Share market volatility → foreign fund flows, foreign market swings, monetary policy changes, liquidity, politics, economic outlook, corporate results.

09-301.r: Dalal Street → Mumbai, home of Bombay Stock Exchange since 1874.

09-302.r: 'Bull' and 'Bear' → share market terms: bull market = prices rising; bear market = prices falling.
09-302.h: A bull tosses up with its horns; a bear swipes down with its paws.

09-303.r: Bear → investor expecting a security's price to fall; sells now, buys back after the fall.

09-304.r: Stock market speculators → Bulls, Bears, Stags, Lame Ducks; a broker is an authorised member trading for customers, not a speculator.

09-305.r: Insider trading → share market dealing using non-public material information; illegal.

09-306.r: Beta → numeric measure of a stock's volatility (systematic risk) relative to the overall market.

09-307.r: Capital market → share market; trades mostly long-term securities like stocks and bonds.

09-308.r: Capital market → government bond market, stock market; money market → call money market, treasury bill market.
09-308.h: Long-term funds = capital market; up to one year = money market.

09-309.r: Most volatile part of organised money market → call money market (funds from overnight to 14 days).
09-309.h: Call money: overnight; notice money: 2 to 14 days.

09-310.r: RBI is not a money market participant; it manages liquidity via LAF. Participants: banks, primary dealers, development finance institutions, mutual funds, NBFCs, corporates.

09-311.r: Commercial Paper → short-term unsecured promissory note; Call Money → overnight inter-bank funds. CDs are issued by banks, not RBI; zero-coupon bonds pay no interest.
